title: The living world and classification
subject: Biology
summary: Living organisms share growth, reproduction, metabolism, response to stimuli and cellular organisation, and are classified by shared features.
points: Taxonomy names and classifies organisms; the hierarchy runs species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom.
Binomial nomenclature gives each species a genus and species name, italicised or underlined.
Museums, herbaria, botanical gardens and zoos preserve reference specimens.
Classification is based on observable characters and evolutionary relationships, so it is revised as evidence grows.
example: Mangifera indica is the binomial name of mango: genus Mangifera, species indica.
mistakes: Writing scientific names without capitalising the genus.
Confusing genus and species.

title: Biological classification
subject: Biology
summary: The five-kingdom system groups organisms as Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
points: Monera covers bacteria and cyanobacteria, which are prokaryotic.
Protista covers unicellular eukaryotes such as amoeba, paramecium and algae.
Fungi are heterotrophic with chitinous cell walls and include moulds, yeasts and mushrooms.
Viruses are not placed in the five kingdoms because they are not cellular and reproduce only inside a host.
Lichens are a symbiotic association of algae and fungi.
example: Yeast is a fungus, not a bacterium, because it is eukaryotic with a chitinous wall.
mistakes: Classifying viruses as bacteria.
Treating algae as plants in the five-kingdom system.

title: Plant kingdom
subject: Biology
summary: Plants are classified into algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms by their body plan and reproductive structures.
points: Algae are mainly aquatic and lack vascular tissue.
Bryophytes are the amphibians of the plant kingdom: they need water for fertilisation and have no true vascular system.
Pteridophytes are the first true vascular plants and reproduce by spores.
Gymnosperms bear naked seeds in cones; angiosperms bear seeds enclosed in fruits and have flowers.
Alternation of generations alternates a haploid gametophyte with a diploid sporophyte.
example: Ferns are pteridophytes: they have vascular tissue but reproduce by spores, not seeds.
mistakes: Calling bryophytes vascular plants.
Saying gymnosperms have no seeds.

title: Animal kingdom
subject: Biology
summary: Animals are classified by symmetry, body cavity, segmentation, notochord and level of organisation.
points: Porifera to echinoderms are invertebrates; chordates include vertebrates with a notochord at some stage.
Symmetry may be radial (cnidarians) or bilateral (most animals).
Coelom may be absent (acoelomate), partial (pseudocoelomate) or true (coelomate).
Vertebrate classes are fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
Arthropods are the largest phylum by number of species.
example: Earthworm is an annelid with true coelom and metameric segmentation.
mistakes: Calling all animals with a backbone chordates only; the notochord definition is broader.
Mixing radial and bilateral symmetry examples.

title: Morphology of flowering plants
subject: Biology
summary: Morphology studies the external form of roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds.
points: Root systems are tap (dicots) or fibrous (monocots); roots may be modified for storage, support or respiration.
Stem modifications include rhizome, tuber, bulb and tendril.
A leaf has lamina, petiole and stipules; venation is reticulate in dicots and parallel in monocots.
A flower has calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium; aestivation and placentation describe their arrangement.
Fruits develop from the ovary and seeds from ovules.

formulas.name: Floral formula
formulas.expr: Br ⊕ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2) describes a family's flower

example: Pea has marginal placentation, while tomato has axile placentation.
mistakes: Confusing a tuber with a bulb.
Forgetting that fruit develops from the ovary, not the ovule.

title: Anatomy of flowering plants
subject: Biology
summary: Plant anatomy studies internal tissue arrangement: epidermis, ground tissue and vascular bundles.
points: Monocot and dicot stems differ in vascular bundle arrangement: scattered versus a ring.
Dicot roots have xylem in a central star with few poles; monocot roots have many xylem poles.
The vascular bundle contains xylem (water upward) and phloem (food in both directions).
Secondary growth from the cambium thickens dicot stems and roots.
example: A transverse section of a monocot stem shows scattered vascular bundles without a cambium ring.
mistakes: Assuming monocots undergo the same secondary growth as dicots.
Mixing the xylem and phloem functions.

title: Structural organisation in animals
subject: Biology
summary: Animal bodies are built from four tissue types — epithelial, connective, muscular and neural — organised into organs and systems.
points: Epithelial tissue covers surfaces and lines cavities; its shape and layering relate to function.
Connective tissue includes loose, dense, cartilage, bone, blood and adipose tissue.
Muscle is skeletal (striated, voluntary), smooth (non-striated, involuntary) or cardiac.
The frog and cockroach are studied as representative animals with organ systems.
example: Blood is a connective tissue because its cells are suspended in a matrix, the plasma.
mistakes: Calling blood an epithelial tissue.
Treating cardiac muscle as voluntary.

title: Cell: the unit of life
subject: Biology
summary: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life, and its organelles carry out specialised jobs.
points: Prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have both.
The plasma membrane is a fluid mosaic of lipids and proteins that controls transport.
Mitochondria produce ATP and chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; both have their own DNA.
Ribosomes make proteins, the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi body process and transport them, and lysosomes digest waste.
The nucleus stores DNA and controls cell activity.
example: A red blood cell has no nucleus, while a liver cell has many mitochondria because it is metabolically active.
mistakes: Saying prokaryotes have no DNA.
Assuming all cells have the same organelle set.

title: Biomolecules
subject: Biology
summary: Living matter is built from carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids, and enzymes catalyse its reactions.
points: Carbohydrates are primary energy sources; cellulose is structural in plants.
Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds and have primary to quaternary structure.
Enzymes are proteins that lower activation energy and are sensitive to temperature and pH.
Nucleic acids store and transmit genetic information; ATP is the energy currency.

formulas.name: Peptide bond
formulas.expr: amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + H₂O

example: Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose, while starch is a glucose polymer.
mistakes: Calling enzymes carbohydrates.
Thinking all lipids are fats.

title: Transport in plants
subject: Biology
summary: Plants move water and minerals upward through xylem and distribute food through phloem.
points: Water moves by osmosis, root pressure and transpiration pull.
Transpiration creates the tension that lifts water through xylem, especially on hot dry days.
Phloem translocates sugars from source to sink using pressure flow.
Plasmolysis, imbibition and water potential explain water movement into and out of cells.
example: A wilted plant recovers after watering because root pressure and transpiration pull restore turgor.
mistakes: Saying xylem carries food.
Thinking phloem transport is one-way only.

title: Mineral nutrition
subject: Biology
summary: Plants need macro and micro nutrients, and deficiency symptoms reveal which element is missing.
points: Macronutrients are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulphur, potassium, calcium and magnesium.
Micronutrients include iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel.
Nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium and cyanobacteria converts atmospheric nitrogen into usable forms.
Deficiency symptoms appear first in older or younger leaves depending on whether the element is mobile.
example: Nitrogen deficiency causes chlorosis and stunted growth because nitrogen is needed for proteins and chlorophyll.
mistakes: Calling all minerals macronutrients.
Assuming deficiency always shows on old leaves.

title: Photosynthesis in higher plants
subject: Biology
summary: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy, producing glucose and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water.
points: Light reactions occur in thylakoids and produce ATP and NADPH while splitting water to release oxygen.
The Calvin cycle in the stroma fixes CO₂ using ATP and NADPH to build carbohydrate.
C4 plants fix CO₂ into a four-carbon acid first, reducing photorespiration in hot climates.
Chlorophyll a is the main pigment; accessory pigments widen the range of light absorbed.
Limiting factors such as light, CO₂ and temperature control the rate.
example: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from water, not from carbon dioxide — shown by isotope experiments.
mistakes: Saying oxygen comes from CO₂.
Believing the dark reaction needs darkness.

title: Respiration in plants
subject: Biology
summary: Plants break down glucose to release energy through glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.
points: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm converts glucose to pyruvate and yields a net 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
Pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle in mitochondria.
The electron transport chain produces most of the ATP, using oxygen as the final electron acceptor.
Anaerobic respiration in plants produces ethanol and CO₂ with much less energy.
The respiratory quotient compares CO₂ released with O₂ used and depends on the substrate.
example: Germinating seeds respire rapidly and release heat, which can be detected with a thermometer in a flask.
mistakes: Claiming plants do not respire at night.
Ignoring that glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm.

title: Plant growth and development
subject: Biology
summary: Plants grow through cell division and elongation, and development is controlled by hormones and environmental signals.
points: Growth is measurable as an increase in size, weight or cell number and follows a sigmoid curve.
Auxins promote elongation and phototropism; cytokinins promote cell division.
Gibberellins promote stem elongation and seed germination; abscisic acid closes stomata and promotes dormancy.
Ethylene ripens fruit and promotes senescence.
Photoperiodism and vernalisation control flowering in many species.
example: Auxin accumulating on the shaded side of a shoot bends it towards light.
mistakes: Calling ethylene a growth promoter only.
Confusing photoperiodism with photosynthesis.

title: Breathing and exchange of gases
subject: Biology
summary: Breathing moves air into the lungs, where oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange between alveoli and blood.
points: Inspiration is active, driven by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles; normal expiration is passive.
Alveoli give a large surface area with thin walls and rich capillaries for gas exchange.
Oxygen travels mainly bound to haemoglobin; carbon dioxide travels mostly as bicarbonate.
Respiratory volume terms include tidal volume, vital capacity and residual volume.
example: At high altitude oxygen partial pressure falls, so breathing rate and red blood cell count rise over time.
mistakes: Confusing breathing with cellular respiration.
Thinking most CO₂ is carried bound to haemoglobin.

title: Body fluids and circulation
subject: Biology
summary: Blood and lymph transport substances, and the heart pumps blood through pulmonary and systemic circuits.
points: Human blood has plasma, red cells, white cells and platelets.
The heart has four chambers; the left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps to the whole body.
The cardiac cycle includes systole and diastole, with valves preventing backflow.
The SA node sets the heart rhythm and the AV node relays the impulse.
Blood groups depend on A, B and Rh antigens and matter for transfusion.
example: A person with O⁻ blood is a universal donor because the red cells carry no A, B or Rh antigens.
mistakes: Saying arteries always carry oxygenated blood; the pulmonary artery does not.
Mixing up systole and diastole.

title: Excretory products and their elimination
subject: Biology
summary: The kidneys filter blood, reabsorb useful substances and excrete nitrogenous waste as urine.
points: The nephron is the functional unit: glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption and secretion.
The loop of Henle creates a concentration gradient that allows urine to be concentrated.
ADH increases water reabsorption; aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption.
Ammonotelic, ureotelic and uricotelic animals excrete different nitrogenous wastes.
Dialysis replaces kidney filtration when kidneys fail.

formulas.name: GFR
formulas.expr: about 125 mL/min in a healthy adult

example: Diabetes insipidus causes large volumes of dilute urine because ADH is deficient.
mistakes: Thinking all reabsorption happens in the glomerulus.
Confusing ADH with aldosterone.

title: Locomotion and movement
subject: Biology
summary: Movement happens when muscles contract and pull on bones across joints.
points: The skeleton has axial (skull, vertebral column, ribs) and appendicular (limbs, girdles) parts.
Muscles work in antagonistic pairs; the biceps flexes and the triceps extends the forearm.
The sliding filament theory explains contraction by actin and myosin filaments sliding past each other.
Joints may be fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial, allowing different ranges of movement.
Disorders include osteoporosis, arthritis, gout and muscular dystrophy.

formulas.name: Sliding filament
formulas.expr: sarcomere shortens as actin slides over myosin

example: During a biceps curl the biceps contracts while the triceps relaxes and lengthens.
mistakes: Saying muscles push bones.
Confusing tendons with ligaments.

title: Neural control and coordination
subject: Biology
summary: The nervous system detects stimuli, processes information and produces rapid responses through neurons.
points: A neuron has dendrites, a cell body and an axon; the axon carries impulses away.
The resting potential is maintained by the sodium–potassium pump and selective permeability.
An action potential is a rapid depolarisation that travels along the axon.
Synapses transmit signals chemically through neurotransmitters.
The brain has forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain regions with distinct functions.
example: A reflex like pulling your hand from a hot pan is fast because the spinal cord responds before the brain.
mistakes: Thinking the impulse is a flow of electrons.
Ignoring the role of myelin in speeding conduction.

title: Chemical coordination and integration
subject: Biology
summary: Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood, which act on target cells to regulate body functions.
points: The pituitary is controlled by the hypothalamus and regulates other glands.
Thyroid hormones control metabolism; insulin and glucagon control blood glucose.
Adrenal hormones prepare the body for stress and regulate salt balance.
Hormones act in small amounts and are usually regulated by feedback loops.
Diabetes mellitus results from insulin deficiency or resistance.
example: After a meal insulin rises and lowers blood glucose; during fasting glucagon raises it.
mistakes: Saying hormones act faster than nerves.
Confusing diabetes mellitus with diabetes insipidus.

title: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
subject: Biology
summary: Flowers contain male and female reproductive organs, and fertilisation produces seeds inside fruits.
points: The anther produces pollen grains; the ovule contains the embryo sac with the egg cell.
Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma and may be self or cross.
Double fertilisation forms a diploid zygote and a triploid endosperm.
After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary the fruit.
Apomixis and polyembryony are exceptions where seeds form without normal fertilisation.

formulas.name: Double fertilisation
formulas.expr: one male gamete + egg → zygote; another + polar nuclei → endosperm

example: In mango, the ovary wall becomes the fruit pulp and the ovule becomes the seed.
mistakes: Saying endosperm is diploid.
Confusing pollination with fertilisation.

title: Reproductive health
subject: Biology
summary: Reproductive health covers safe reproduction, contraception, prevention of sexually transmitted infections and assisted reproduction.
points: Contraceptive methods include barrier, hormonal, intrauterine and surgical approaches.
Sexually transmitted infections such as HIV, syphilis and gonorrhoea need early treatment.
Infertility treatments include IVF, ZIFT, GIFT and artificial insemination.
Awareness, counselling and prenatal care reduce maternal and infant risk.
Sex determination in humans is chromosomal: XX female, XY male, decided by the father's sperm.
example: IVF fertilises the egg outside the body and transfers the embryo into the uterus.
mistakes: Treating reproductive health as only about pregnancy.
Believing the mother determines the child's sex.

title: Evolution
subject: Biology
summary: Evolution is the change in inherited characteristics of populations over generations, driven by natural selection and other mechanisms.
points: Darwin's natural selection favours variations that improve survival and reproduction.
Evidence comes from fossils, comparative anatomy, embryology, biochemistry and biogeography.
Homologous structures share ancestry; analogous structures share function but not ancestry.
Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium describes allele frequencies in an ideal non-evolving population.
Speciation occurs when populations become reproductively isolated.
example: Antibiotic resistance spreads because resistant bacteria survive treatment and reproduce.
mistakes: Saying individuals evolve rather than populations.
Treating evolution as progress towards a goal.

title: Microbes in human welfare
subject: Biology
summary: Microorganisms are used in food, medicine, agriculture and sewage treatment, though some cause disease.
points: Lactic acid bacteria curdle milk into curd; yeast ferments dough and beverages.
Antibiotics such as penicillin come from fungi and bacteria.
Biofertilisers like Rhizobium and Azotobacter add nitrogen to soil.
Sewage treatment uses aerobic and anaerobic microbes to break down waste.
Biogas is produced by methanogens from organic waste.
example: Penicillin was discovered from the mould Penicillium notatum.
mistakes: Assuming all microbes are harmful.
Confusing biofertiliser with chemical fertiliser.

title: Principles and processes of biotechnology
subject: Biology
summary: Biotechnology uses living systems or their parts to make useful products, using tools such as restriction enzymes, vectors and PCR.
points: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific recognition sequences.
Plasmids are common vectors that carry foreign DNA into host cells.
PCR amplifies DNA through denaturation, annealing and extension cycles.
Recombinant DNA is inserted into a host, selected and expressed.
Bioreactors allow large-scale culture of cells or enzymes.
example: Human insulin is produced by bacteria carrying the human insulin gene on a plasmid.
mistakes: Thinking PCR needs living cells.
Confusing a vector with a host organism.

title: Biotechnology and its applications
subject: Biology
summary: Biotechnology is applied in medicine, agriculture and industry, including GM crops, gene therapy and transgenic animals.
points: Bt cotton carries a bacterial gene that protects it from bollworm.
Gene therapy replaces a faulty gene, as in severe combined immunodeficiency.
Transgenic animals are used for research, medicine production and safety testing.
RNA interference silences specific genes and is used against pests.
Ethical and biosafety issues surround GM organisms and gene editing.
example: Bt cotton produces a toxin harmful to specific insect larvae but not to humans.
mistakes: Believing Bt toxin harms all insects.
Thinking gene therapy edits every cell of the body.

title: Ecosystem
subject: Biology
summary: An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with each other and their physical environment, with energy flowing and nutrients cycling.
points: Producers capture energy, consumers transfer it along food chains, and decomposers return nutrients.
Energy flow is unidirectional and only about 10% passes to the next trophic level.
Ecological pyramids show numbers, biomass or energy at each trophic level.
Nutrient cycles such as carbon and nitrogen move matter between organisms and the environment.
Primary productivity sets the energy budget of an ecosystem.

formulas.name: Ten percent law
formulas.expr: energy at next level ≈ 10% of the previous level

example: A grassland supports many more herbivores than a forest supports top carnivores because energy shrinks at each level.
mistakes: Assuming energy cycles like nutrients.
Counting decomposers as a trophic level of consumers in every pyramid.

title: Biodiversity and conservation
subject: Biology
summary: Biodiversity is the variety of species, genes and ecosystems, and conserving it protects ecosystem services and future options.
points: Species diversity is highest in the tropics because of stable climate and long evolutionary history.
Loss of habitat, overexploitation, invasive species and pollution drive extinction.
In-situ conservation keeps species in their habitat through national parks and biosphere reserves.
Ex-situ conservation keeps species outside their habitat in zoos, seed banks and botanical gardens.
Hotspots and the species–area relationship guide conservation priorities.

formulas.name: Species–area relationship
formulas.expr: log S = log C + z log A

example: The Western Ghats is a biodiversity hotspot with many endemic species found nowhere else.
mistakes: Thinking biodiversity means only the number of species.
Assuming ex-situ conservation is enough on its own.
